headline: Erdafitinib
punch: It grew a child's long bones. It also bent his spine.

headline: What it actually is
body: An oral pan-FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor, the first FDA-approved in its class, licensed for urothelial carcinoma. Pan means it hits FGFR1, 2, 3 and 4 rather than picking one. | The height interest comes from FGFR3: it brakes chondrocyte proliferation, so inhibiting it should release that brake. The logic is sound and there is a human case telling you exactly what happens.
punch: Blocking the brake. All four of them.

headline: It works on human bone
body: Majlessipour 2024. A pre-pubescent child with an FGFR1-mutated glioma was treated with erdafitinib, and the tumour responded. | While on treatment the patient experienced **rapid skeletal and long bone overgrowth**. The authors describe the pattern as strikingly reminiscent of people with congenital loss-of-function FGFR3 mutations. So the mechanism translates into a human growing long bone.
punch: The mechanism is real in a human.

headline: And the same sentence
body: Read their wording in full: rapid skeletal and long bone overgrowth **resulting in kyphoscoliosis**. The paper's own framing is that this is **the first detailed report of a serious adverse effect**. | The growth and the deformity are not two findings. They are one finding described in one clause. Uncontrolled long bone overgrowth in a growing spine is what kyphoscoliosis is.
punch: ==The growth and the deformity are the same event.==

headline: Why it deforms
body: Erdafitinib's toxicity profile is largely attributed to **FGFR1** inhibition, and FGFR1 is engaged *before* FGFR3 is fully hit, because the drug is more potent at FGFR1. | So you cannot dose it up to properly release the FGFR3 brake without first saturating a receptor that is doing something else. The adult toxicities, hyperphosphatemia, skin and nail damage, hand-foot syndrome, come from the same place.
punch: You hit the wrong receptor first, by design.

headline: You cannot monitor it
body: Whether an FGFR-pathway drug is actually active on a given person's growth plates **can only be confirmed by serial bone-age X-ray**. No serum marker reports it. | So you are running a drug whose therapeutic effect and whose deformity risk are the same process, with no real-time readout of either. By the time an X-ray shows you, the thing it shows is already built.
punch: No marker. Only an X-ray, afterwards.

headline: Selectivity is the answer
body: If the problem is FGFR1, the fix is a drug that does not hit FGFR1. TYRA-300 is FGFR3-selective and was tested in three genetic contexts: wild-type mice, an achondroplasia model, and a hypochondroplasia model. | **In each model it increased nasoanal length and tibia and femur length**, including in wild-type animals. Histology showed increased chondrocyte proliferation and differentiation.
punch: Selective beat pan, in the model.

headline: But that is mouse
body: TYRA-300's data is mouse. Erdafitinib's bone data is one human child on oncology treatment. Neither is a trial in anyone trying to get taller. | The honest read is that FGFR3 is a real target and erdafitinib is the wrong molecule for it, with the right molecule still in animals. That is a statement about compound choice, not about whether to run one.
punch: Right target. Wrong molecule. The right one is preclinical.

headline: Interactions
body: Erdafitinib is a **CYP3A4 and CYP2C9 substrate** and it **inhibits P-glycoprotein and OCT2**. In a stack containing letrozole, telmisartan, lemborexant or cialis, all of which touch CYP3A4, that is a live interaction surface rather than a footnote. | And there is no human evidence base for combining it with vosoritide outside paediatric genetic disease.
punch: It sits in the middle of a CYP3A4 traffic jam.

headline: Verdict
body: It demonstrably grows human long bone, which almost nothing else on this list can claim. It demonstrated it by deforming a child's spine, in a paper written to report that as an adverse event. | The pathway is right and the molecule is wrong: pan-FGFR means FGFR1 saturates first, and you cannot see what it is doing without an X-ray. The selective version exists and is still in mice.
punch: Proof of concept and cautionary tale, in one patient.
